verses.text: Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
Now I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you.
But I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.
Every man praying or prophesying, having his head covered, dishonoureth his head.
But every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven.
For if the woman be not covered, let her also be shorn: but if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered.
For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, forasmuch as he is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man.
For the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man.
Neither was the man created for the woman; but the woman for the man.
For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels.
Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord.
For as the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things of God.
Judge in yourselves: is it comely that a woman pray unto God uncovered?
Doth not even nature itself teach you, that, if a man have long hair, it is a shame unto him?
But if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering.
But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God.
Now in this that I declare unto you I praise you not, that ye come together not for the better, but for the worse.
For first of all, when ye come together in the church, I hear that there be divisions among you; and I partly believe it.
For there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you.
When ye come together therefore into one place, this is not to eat the Lord’s supper.
For in eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken.
What? have ye not houses to eat and to drink in? or despise ye the church of God, and shame them that have not? What shall I say to you? shall I praise you in this? I praise you not.
For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread:
And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come.
Wherefore whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.
For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep.
For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.
But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world.
Wherefore, my brethren, when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another.
And if any man hunger, let him eat at home; that ye come not together unto condemnation. And the rest will I set in order when I come.

summary: "Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ" closes the long argument about liberty and opens a new one about assembly. Paul begins with praise — "I praise you, brethren, that ye remember me in all things, and keep the ordinances, as I delivered them to you" — and then takes up the first of two things that go wrong when the Corinthians gather. The first is a matter of dress and of order. "I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God." From this comes the rule: a man who prays or prophesies "having his head covered, dishonoureth his head," while "every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven." Paul reasons from creation — the man "is the image and glory of God: but the woman is the glory of the man," since "the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man" — and adds the odd, unexplained clause that the woman ought "to have power on her head because of the angels." Then, having drawn the asymmetry, he immediately refuses to let it become independence: "Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things of God." He appeals to their own judgment and to what "nature itself" teaches about long hair, noting that a woman's hair "is given her for a covering," and closes the section by declining to argue further: "But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God." The second problem draws no praise at all. "Now in this that I declare unto you I praise you not, that ye come together not for the better, but for the worse." There are "divisions among you," which Paul partly believes, and which he says will serve to show "they which are approved"; but the result is that "when ye come together therefore into one place, this is not to eat the Lord's supper." Each brings his own food and eats it first, "and one is hungry, and another is drunken" — a supper that reproduces the class divisions of the city inside the church. Paul's rebuke is scalding: "have ye not houses to eat and to drink in? or despise ye the church of God, and shame them that have not?" Against this he sets the tradition he received and handed on: "For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me. After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me." The rite is not private and not merely retrospective: "as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come." From this follows the warning: "whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord," so "let a man examine himself, and so let him eat." To eat "unworthily" is to eat "damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body," and Paul says the consequences are already visible: "For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep." Yet even this judgment is fatherly — "when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" — and the practical remedy is almost disappointingly plain: "when ye come together to eat, tarry one for another. And if any man hunger, let him eat at home; that ye come not together unto condemnation. And the rest will I set in order when I come."
takeaways: Paul frames both halves of this chapter as handed-down tradition rather than personal opinion. He praises them for keeping "the ordinances, as I delivered them to you," and introduces the Supper with the formula "I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you." The verbs are those of careful transmission, and they place the words of institution among the earliest Christian material we possess — written down years before any Gospel, describing what happened "the same night in which he was betrayed." Whatever a reader concludes about the practices at issue, Paul is not inventing them; he is passing on a deposit and correcting a church that has drifted from it.

The head-covering argument is easy to caricature and harder to read carefully, because Paul builds the asymmetry and then blocks its abuse in the same breath. He does say "the head of the woman is the man"; he also says "the head of Christ is God," which puts headship inside the life of God rather than in the category of superiority and inferiority. He argues from the order of creation, and then adds "Nevertheless neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as the woman is of the man, even so is the man also by the woman; but all things of God." And the whole passage assumes without comment that women pray and prophesy aloud in the assembly — the question at issue is how, not whether.

The way the section ends is as instructive as its content. After appeals to creation, to the angels, to nature, and to their own judgment, Paul finishes with "if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God." He is willing to state a practice, give reasons for it, and then decline to fight about it, resting the case on the settled usage of the churches rather than on further argument. Contentiousness is treated as the real disorder; a man determined to quarrel about head coverings has already lost the point of the assembly he is quarrelling in.

The Corinthian abuse of the Supper is not doctrinal error but social contempt, and Paul treats the two as inseparable. "In eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken" — the wealthy eat their provisions while the poor, arriving late from work, get nothing. Paul's verdict is that this cancels the sacrament: "this is not to eat the Lord's supper." The identical words and elements, used in a gathering that shames "them that have not," do not produce the Lord's supper at all. A rite that divides the body while claiming to be the body has become its own contradiction, which is why the remedy is as concrete as the sin: "tarry one for another."

"Ye do shew the Lord's death till he come" gives the rite three tenses at once. It reaches back to a night that can be dated and named; it does something in the present, since to "shew" is to proclaim publicly rather than to recall privately; and it is bounded by a future — "till he come" — so that every celebration is provisional and points past itself. Remembrance in this sense is not nostalgia for an absent friend but the Church's standing public announcement of a death, made by eating and drinking, and made repeatedly "as often as" she gathers.

The warnings in the final verses assume that something more than bread is at stake. To eat "unworthily" is not to be insufficiently holy — no one would ever eat on those terms — but to eat in the manner Paul has just described, and the charge is startlingly severe: such a person is "guilty of the body and blood of the Lord." The prescribed response is self-examination rather than abstention: "let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread." The diagnosis is failure at "discerning the Lord's body," and even the resulting sickness and death among them are read as correction rather than condemnation — "when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world." Judgment inside the Church is presented as mercy at work.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 2:22-23 — she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man
crossRefs.why: Paul's premises in verses 8 and 9 are lifted directly from this narrative: "the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man," and "neither was the man created for the woman; but the woman for the man." The source passage also supplies the counterweight he adds in verse 11, since the woman is made because "it is not good that the man should be alone" and is greeted as "bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" — mutual belonging, not mere derivation.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 3:28 — there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus
crossRefs.why: The sharpest internal tension in reading this chapter is between the created-order argument here and the baptismal declaration there, and both are Paul's. His own bridge is verse 11, "neither is the man without the woman, neither the woman without the man, in the Lord," where the phrase "in the Lord" does the same work as "in Christ Jesus" does in Galatians. How far that oneness reshapes the ordering described here is precisely where interpreters divide.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 12:14 — this day shall be unto you for a memorial... by an ordinance for ever
crossRefs.why: "This do in remembrance of me" is spoken at a Passover meal, and the Passover was itself commanded as a perpetual memorial in which each generation was to count itself among those brought out of Egypt. Reading the institution against its background shows that biblical remembrance is a liturgical act with present effect rather than a mental exercise, and it explains why Paul can move so quickly from a supper to a covenant: the meal in Exodus was where a delivered people learned who they were.

crossRefs.label: Luke 22:19-20 — This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me
crossRefs.why: Of the Gospel accounts this is the closest to Paul's, sharing both "this do in remembrance of me" and the description of the cup as "the new testament in my blood." The agreement of two independent early witnesses on the same wording indicates a fixed liturgical form already in use, and Luke's setting — "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer" — supplies the context Paul assumes but does not state.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 — is it not the communion of the body of Christ?... we being many are one bread, and one body
crossRefs.why: The previous chapter states the principle this one applies. There Paul argues that sharing the cup and the bread joins the participants to Christ and to each other, "for we are all partakers of that one bread"; here he confronts a church whose manner of eating denies exactly that. The two passages together explain why humiliating the poor at the meal is not a lapse of manners but a failure at "discerning the Lord's body."

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 10:29 — hath counted the blood of the covenant... an unholy thing
crossRefs.why: The same logic of aggravated guilt appears there: contempt shown toward the blood of the covenant is treated as an offence of a different order than ordinary transgression. It illuminates Paul's charge that one who eats unworthily is "guilty of the body and blood of the Lord," and it shares the assumption that severe warnings belong inside the Church, addressed to people already sanctified, rather than to outsiders.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes the head-covering passage as a genuine apostolic tradition — Paul explicitly praises the Corinthians for keeping "the ordinances, as I delivered them to you" — while distinguishing within it between an abiding principle and a disciplinary form. The abiding element is the created order Paul argues from, the differentiation of man and woman as willed by God and as bearing meaning in worship, together with the reverence and modesty proper to the assembly. The form, a veil on the head, is a custom the Church has authority to require, adapt, or relax, and in fact veiling was general church practice for many centuries before being left free in modern times. This is offered as an ordinary example of how the Church handles a scriptural directive: the apostolic principle is preserved, while the concrete discipline that expresses it is governed by the living authority of the Church, which is also how Paul himself concludes the matter, by appealing to the settled usage of "the churches of God" rather than to further argument. On "the head of the woman is the man," the tradition reads headship in light of "the head of Christ is God," that is, as an order of relation within an equality of nature, not a difference of dignity.

counterpoint.summary: Protestants divide, and the division does not track the usual lines. One reading holds that Paul grounds the practice in creation, angels, and nature rather than in local custom, and that the covering therefore remains binding wherever the passage is obeyed; a minority of congregations still practice it. A far more common reading holds that the covering was a first-century cultural signal of respectability whose meaning has not survived, so that obeying Paul today means honouring the principle of orderly, non-provocative, reverent worship in whatever the local equivalent may be — and points out that Paul himself appeals to "nature" and to their own judgment, arguments that assume shared cultural intuitions. Both readings resist the idea that an ecclesiastical authority may bind or loose the practice on its own authority, holding instead that the text's own distinction between principle and form must be discerned from Scripture. Egalitarian and complementarian Protestants further divide over "the head of the woman is the man," the first pressing verses 11-12 and the fact that women here pray and prophesy publicly, the second pressing verses 3-9 as a permanent ordering of roles. All agree the passage assumes women's audible participation in worship.

interpretationNotes.claim: On the words of institution, Catholic reading takes "this is my body, which is broken for you" and "This cup is the new testament in my blood" in their plain sense: what is given is Christ Himself under the forms of bread and wine. "This do in remembrance of me" is read as a command that constitutes an office as well as a rite — a charge given to the apostles to do what He did — and the remembrance it commands is understood in the biblical sense of memorial, in which a past saving act is made present to those who keep it, as the Passover made the exodus present to every generation. Hence the Church's teaching that the Eucharist does not repeat Calvary but makes the one sacrifice present; "ye do shew the Lord's death till he come" is read as a proclamation that does what it says. The tradition also draws from this passage the practice of receiving with reverence and preparation, and from Paul's careful language of receiving and delivering, the conviction that the liturgy is something handed on rather than devised.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings again span a range. Sacramental Protestants hold that Christ truly gives Himself to the faithful receiver in the Supper, so that the words are not empty, while declining any account of a change in the elements. Reformed readings emphasize that believers are lifted by the Spirit to feed on Christ, who remains the ascended Lord; the presence is real but not local, and "till he come" is taken to imply that He is bodily absent in the interim. Memorialist readings take "in remembrance of me" as its own explanation and read the Supper as a solemn, covenantal act of remembering and proclaiming. Common Protestant textual observations are that Paul continues to call the element "this bread" after the institution, and that a memorial and a sacrifice are different categories. Both traditions agree that the Supper was instituted by Christ, that its words come with dominical authority, that it proclaims His death publicly, and that it looks forward to His return.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "whosoever shall eat this bread, and drink this cup of the Lord, unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord" as evidence for the objective reality of what is received: one cannot be guilty of a body and blood that are not there. Correspondingly "not discerning the Lord's body" is read primarily as a failure to recognize what the sacrament is. From this the Church derives a real discipline — that grave sin should be repented and, where it is mortal, sacramentally confessed before receiving; that the community may and must regulate admission to communion; and that the fitting posture toward the sacrament is reverence and preparation rather than casual approach. The bodily consequences Paul reports, that "many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep," are taken at face value as chastisement, and read together with "we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" as a picture of purifying discipline within the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally take "not discerning the Lord's body" in light of the abuse that occasioned the whole passage, and understand the body being failed as the Church — the poor who are shamed are the body of Christ that the Corinthians are not recognizing. Read this way, the sin Paul condemns is not irreverence toward the elements but contempt for the gathered people, which is why his remedy is "tarry one for another" rather than any change in the rite. On worthiness, they emphasize that Paul's instruction is to examine and then eat, not to examine and then abstain, and that the qualification for the table is faith and repentance rather than absolution granted through a priest; the Supper is given to sinners who know themselves such. Many Protestant traditions nonetheless practise a form of fencing the table and call for self-examination and reconciliation beforehand, and some read the passage as Catholics do, taking reverence toward the sacrament itself to be at issue. Both traditions agree that the warning is real, that the Supper is not to be approached carelessly, and that Paul's judgment language is corrective and aimed at saving rather than destroying.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
